INTRODUCTION (no heading)

Explain the idea behind your study and why it matters. Include a theory or mechanism that could explain why screen time and mind wandering might be associated, and cite your sources.

End with your research question, then your null hypothesis (H0) and your alternative hypothesis (H1). Name both variables and say what relationship you expect.

TENSE
- Present tense for definitions, theories and established knowledge (Mind wandering is ...).
- Past tense for specific earlier studies (Smith (2020) found ...) and for your hypotheses (We hypothesised that ...).
- Your pre-registration was written in the future tense (We will measure ...). Change it to the past tense when you reuse it.

CITING SOURCES IN YOUR TEXT
- One author: Smith (2020) found ..., or ... (Smith, 2020).
- Two authors: Smith and Jones (2020) found ..., or ... (Smith & Jones, 2020).
- Three or more authors: Smith et al. (2020) found ..., or ... (Smith et al., 2020).

# Results

```{=html}
<!--
Start by presenting your data. Report descriptive statistics for each variable (in the text or in a table), and include a figure that helps the reader see the pattern.

Then report the correlation that tests your hypothesis, including the checks you were taught. Put your analysis code in code blocks, before or alongside the text that reports it.

State whether you reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis (never "accept"), and what this means for your alternative hypothesis. Do not interpret the finding here; that comes in the Discussion.

Use the past tense for your findings (... was positively correlated with ...) and the present tense when pointing to a table or figure (Table 1 shows ...).

REPORTING NUMBERS AND STATISTICS (APA 7)
- Put statistical symbols in italics: *M*, *SD*, *N*, *r*, *p*. Use *N* for the whole sample and *n* for a part of it.
- Put spaces around =, < and >: *r*(48) = -.32. Degrees of freedom go in brackets after the test symbol.
- No zero before the decimal point for values that cannot be greater than 1, such as *r* and *p*: *r* = .32, *p* = .024. Use a zero for values that can be greater than 1: *M* = 0.85.
- Round *r* to two and *p* to three decimal places. If *p* is smaller than .001, write *p* < .001. Report the exact *p* otherwise.
- For means and standard deviations for integer-scale data (e.g., surveys): one decimal, and two decimals for other means and SDs. Use the same number of decimals for the same measure throughout. Your output will show many more digits; do not copy them all.
- Report a confidence interval with the correlation: 95% CI [.05, .55]. Put both limits inside square brackets.
- Write numbers below 10 as words (six participants) and 10 and above as numerals (24 participants). Use numerals for statistics, measurements, ages and points on a scale, even below 10, and never start a sentence with a numeral.

TABLES AND FIGURES
- Number each one (Table 1, Figure 1) and refer to it by number in your text.
- For a table, put the number in bold on one line, then the title in italics, in title case, on the line below, both above the table. Use as few lines as possible and no vertical lines.
- For a figure, the number (bold) and title (italics) go above the figure. Label the axes clearly, with units.
-->
```

# Discussion

```{=html}
<!--
Answer your research question first, in plain words, using your result. Do not repeat statistics to do this, just words.
Relate your finding to key findings in the literature: does it fit them, and what might explain any difference?
Evaluate your study critically: who took part and how they were recruited, how each concept was measured, and why a correlation cannot show cause. For each point, say how it affects what you can conclude.
End with a take-home message that goes no further than your data allow.
Use the past tense for your findings and those of other studies, and the present tense for interpretation and your take-home message (This suggests ...).
-->
```
